sourceInformation.source: Pitfall II: Lost Caverns (1984), David Crane / Activision
sourceInformation.perspective: 2.5D side view with an orthographic camera
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js r180 (0.180.0), WebGPURenderer with WebGL 2 recovery; Rapier 2D 0.19.3; Gamepad API; Web Audio API; PeerJS 1.5.5; AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.4.0; native HTML/CSS/JavaScript; Bun bundler. A local r180 async-pipeline rejection patch enables renderer recovery.
sourceInformation.artDirection: Original procedural 3D cel shading, inverted-hull ink outlines, cut-rock caverns, warm expedition illustration, botanical details, and restrained paper grain
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer, AnimationClip and native keyframe tracks for idle, run, jump, climb, swim, balloon flight, waving, fox tail and creature wingbeats; procedural secondary effects
sourceInformation.audio: Original code-synthesized adaptive marimba/flute/bass adventure music at 10% default volume, procedural effects and ambient percussion; formant-filtered Animalese-style rescue gibberish; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: 1–4-player ghost expedition races through AI Hub; standalone room races with WebRTC/PeerJS public signaling and a BroadcastChannel local transport
sourceInformation.testing: One-command headless Chromium suite: software WebGPU and WebGL 2; 2,895-step complete physics playthrough; every enemy and balloon pop; score/rewind persistence; native animation; developer tools; offline file launch with network blocked; emulated standard controller; actual synthetic multitouch; offline and live audio signal; WebRTC on isolated browser contexts using a loopback signaling server; BroadcastChannel rooms; official AI Hub harness with 2 and 4 seats, 150 ms latency, 50 ms jitter, 5% packet loss, time-up and host departure; composition screenshots. Physical controller, real mobile hardware, subjective listening and public signaling service availability: unknown.
sourceInformation.research: Activision's 1984 Atari 2600 manual (AtariAge transcription), AtariAge screenshots and game profile, original manual/advertising excerpts: connected cavern layout, ladders, swimming, balloon rides, rear-approach rat, rescue objectives, healing checkpoints, score penalties, creature movement, contextual music and diary tone. AI Hub protocol and client; Three.js r180 source; Rapier documentation and pinned API definitions
sourceInformation.environment: Codex CLI (headless); Linux / Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2

testingFeedback: Four issues: bundle replacement syntax, a stalled graphics startup on GPU pipeline rejection, oversized visual effects, and transient gameplay text showing through the title. All corrected. Additional code-review findings for free flight, mouse activity and fall scoring are covered by verification.
Two: the initial bundle could not start, and a rejected graphics pipeline could block four-player Hub readiness.
The scripted complete expedition through actual Rapier physics, combined with the official four-player Hub harness under packet loss and host departure.
The first WebGPU screenshot was captured before a trustworthy visible frame. State assertions and WebGL 2 composition captures provided useful evidence instead.
engineFeedback: Native AnimationMixer clips, procedural geometry and toon materials make a cohesive illustrated expedition possible in one file.
Yes. r180 compileAsync could remain unresolved after a native GPU pipeline rejection during multi-copy headless testing. Reading the pinned engine source identified the missing rejection path.
The traversal state machine, expedition/score systems, controller-first menus, procedural audio, touch assistance and ghost-race networking.
Recovering from software WebGPU device/pipeline failures while meeting the Hub readiness deadline, and validating visual composition when WebGPU screenshots were unreliable.

Patched r180 WebGPUPipelineUtils to forward createRenderPipelineAsync rejection into its awaited promise. This lets the application catch the error and recover to WebGL 2 instead of hanging startup. No other engine changes.
Make renderer initialization and asynchronous pipeline failures reject reliably, with a standard backend-recovery path.
promptFeedback: The specific source, procedural audio requirement and 10-foot controller-first direction give the expedition a coherent identity.
Standalone multiplayer transport and the exact scope of the feedback fields were open to interpretation.
Integrating every traversal mechanic, polished procedural art, standalone networking and the complete hub lifecycle into a single offline-capable file.
Specify whether standalone multiplayer should use a public signaling service, manual signaling or a supplied server.

aiHub.name: The Great Below-About
aiHub.tagline: A little lost. A long way down.
aiHub.description: An ink-and-cel expedition through fern caves, eel-filled rivers and a balloon belfry. Find two missing friends and the Sunseed Prism, or race up to three ghost explorers for the best haul.
aiHub.controls: WASD / arrows or left stick: move, climb, swim and steer; Space / Cross: jump; E / Square: release balloon; M / Triangle: map; Esc / Options: pause; touch: drag left half and tap right half.
